## How they got there
Manchester City secured the title by beating Inter 1-0 in the final after navigating through 16 knockout teams. Their profile was defined by an attacking intensity that saw them generate 69.2 attacks per game, a figure better than this 100% of that season's group/league-phase teams and 99% of all Champions League teams since 2011-12. This dominance in ball circulation complemented their approach, as they averaged 734 passes per game to control possession at 64.2%, ranking better than this 100% of that season's group/league-phase teams and 92% of all Champions League teams since 2011-12.

## Would the model have picked them?
The verdict indicates that the model would not have picked Manchester City, as they ranked 3rd among knockout teams despite being a leading contender outside the model's top two. While the base rate suggests a random knockout team has only a 12.5% chance of reaching the final, the model assigned a probability of 27.1%, placing them third in that specific ranking. The expected stage on the scale nearest to the model's expectation was semi-finals, reflecting an anticipated outcome lower than their actual victory.

## Weak spots
The team displayed a clear weak spot in long passing, where they executed only 9.1% of passes as long balls, a rate better than this 12% of that season's group/league-phase teams and just 7% of all Champions League teams since 2011-12. This specific metric contributed negatively to the model's prediction by -0.16 knockout stages, alongside lower contributions from distance covered per game at 116.2 km and opponent shots per game at 5.0. These areas represented the fewest beaten first among their statistical profile for that season.

messages.content: You are a football performance analyst writing for a curious, data-literate reader. Use ONLY the facts provided. Quote every number exactly as it appears in the facts, with the same rounding. Do not introduce players, managers, matches, events, analyses or numbers that are not in the facts. 'Better than this %' figures say how many teams the club beat on a stat, so higher is always better, including for stats marked '(lower is better)', where beating a team means having the lower value. Write them as 'better than X% of teams', never as 'top X%'. SHAP contributions are measured in knockout stages: a positive contribution means the stat pushed the model's expected stage up by that fraction of a round, a negative one pushed it down. A SHAP contribution is the model's view, not a measure of how good the team was at the stat: a team can rank high on a stat the model marked down, so never call a stat a strength or a weakness because of its SHAP sign. Everything here is a statistical association, not a cause: never say a stat or a team's profile drove, powered, propelled, carried, helped, hindered or prevented a result, and do not explain why a stat got its contribution. Write plain markdown without tables.
